deltaNote: JULY 2026 (released Aug 26): Headline PCE 3.7% YoY (+0.2% MoM), 0.1pp above the Dow Jones consensus. Core PCE 3.3% YoY (+0.2% MoM), matching consensus and flat vs June's 3.3% (down from May's cycle-high 3.4%). Personal income +0.4% MoM; spending +0.2% MoM; saving rate 3.0%. label: Fed Funds Rate
value: 3.50–3.75%; September 15-16 Hike Odds at ~57.5% as Bond Rout and Soft ADP Data Pull in Opposite Directions
source: Federal Reserve FOMC, July 29 2026 (held); Warsh Jackson Hole Keynote, Aug 28 2026; CME FedWatch, Sept 2 2026
delta: Held at 3.50-3.75% since July 29; Sept 15-16 hike odds held near ~57.5% into Sept 2 even as ADP showed private payrolls slowing sharply to 38,000 in August
deltaNote: AUG 28 UPDATE: Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote as Chair (his 100th day in the role) turned notably hawkish — he said inflation remains 'above our 2 percent target,' called price stability the Fed's 'predominant focus,' and said the Fed 'may have work to do' on rates, while also stepping back from forward guidance ('you can call it an outline, you can call it a trail map, just don't call it forward guidance'). CME FedWatch September hike odds jumped to ~57% from ~35% pre-speech; the 2-year Treasury yield rose to ~4.32%, its highest since July. SEPT 2 UPDATE: ADP's National Employment Report showed private payrolls rose just 38,000 in August (vs 48,000 forecast, down from July's revised 46,000) — the slowest pace since January — a labor-softening signal that would normally cool hike bets, but September odds held near 57.5% as the global bond yield rout (10Y at 4.814%, highest since Nov 2023) and renewed Mideast-driven oil spike kept inflation-hawk pressure on the Fed ahead of the Sept 16-17 FOMC. Prior: July 28-29 FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% with 3 hawkish dissents.

label: US 10Y / 30Y Treasury Yield
value: 10Y Hits 4.814% (Sept 2) — Highest Since Nov 2023; 30Y 5.31-5.32% (Aug 17 Peak) — Highest Since 2007
source: CNBC / Federal Reserve H.15 / FRED / Yahoo Finance; July 23 - September 2, 2026
delta: Renewed US-Iran strikes near the Strait of Hormuz (Aug 31-Sept 1) pushed oil and yields sharply higher; the 10Y hit 4.814% intraday Sept 2 as part of a synchronized global bond rout (Japan 10Y >3% for the first time since 1996, German Bund highest since 2011, UK gilts highest since 2008).
deltaNote: AUG 31-SEPT 2 ARC: Warsh's Aug 28 hawkish Jackson Hole keynote lifted the 2-year to ~4.32%; an Aug 31 US strike on Iranian rocket launchers near the Strait of Hormuz then sent Brent back above $90 and yields toward their highest since January 2025. Overnight Aug 31-Sept 1, two oil tankers were struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, driving Brent to $94.65 (+4.6%) and WTI to $90.22 (+5.2%) on Sept 1 — the 10Y rose to 4.792%, a 20-month high, its fifth straight session of gains. The selloff extended Sept 2: the 10Y touched 4.814% intraday (highest since Nov 2023) as the rout went global — Japan's 10Y crossed 3% for the first time since 1996, Germany's Bund hit 3.375% (highest since 2011), and UK gilts extended a post-2008 high to 5.25%. The 30-year's Aug 17 peak of 5.31-5.32% (highest since June 2007) remains the cycle high. National debt concerns (nearing $40T) and stubborn above-target inflation remain the structural floor under long-end yields; equities shrugged off the rout Sept 2, with the S&P 500 and Dow each rebounding ~0.47%.

label: Michigan Consumer Sentiment (August 2026 Final)
delta: +0.7 vs preliminary (51.0); still -6.3% vs July final (55.2)
deltaNote: AUG 2026 FINAL (released Aug 28): 51.7, revised up from the 51.0 preliminary but still down 6.3% from July's final 55.2 and roughly 11% below a year ago. Current Economic Conditions fell 5.3% to 51.9; Consumer Expectations fell 7.0% to 51.5. One-year inflation expectations eased to 4.0% (from 4.2% preliminary); long-run expectations held at 3.3% for a third straight month. Sentiment fell across all political groups, sharpest among Republicans, older consumers, and lower/middle-income households. Still well above May 2026's all-time record low of 44.8, but the reading — alongside July retail sales' steepest drop in over a year — underscores the crack in the 'resilient consumer' narrative that Warsh's same-day hawkish Jackson Hole keynote did nothing to ease.

The selloff deepened Sept 1 after two tankers were struck in the Strait of Hormuz overnight — Dow -0.79%, S&P -0.71%, Nasdaq -1.03% — alongside a soft ISM Manufacturing PMI (54.6%, down from 55.6%) and a 20-month-high 10-year Treasury yield (4.792%). Equities then shrugged off a synchronized global bond yield rout on Sept 2 (US 10Y to 4.814%, highest since Nov 2023; Japan 10Y above 3% for the first time since 1996; German Bund and UK gilts at multi-year highs) to close broadly higher, even as ADP showed private payrolls slowing sharply to 38,000 in August.

label: US Avg Effective Tariff Rate
value: Canada Section 338 Tariffs (50% on ~$20B) Took Effect Aug 22; Canada Retaliates With 15-50% Tariffs on $20B, Effective Sept 8
source: USTR / Global Trade Alert / Bloomberg / AP; July 24 - August 25, 2026
contestNote: US-Canada trade talks collapsed late Aug 21; the Section 338 tariffs (50% on ~$20B of Canadian autos, alcohol, and dairy) took effect Aug 22 (after a brief 3-day suspension from the original Aug 19 date). Carney declared Canada 'at war' with the US on trade. On Aug 25, Carney announced Canada's countermeasures: tiered 15%/25%/50% retaliatory tariffs on ~$20B of US goods across 700+ products (steel, aluminum, furniture, clothing at 50%; appliances, dairy, seafood at 25%; other industrial goods at 15%), effective September 8, plus a C$7.5B (US$5.4B) support package for affected workers and businesses. Two days later (Aug 24) Trump additionally threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, auto parts, and steel starting Jan 1, 2027. Separately, the Section 122/Section 301 transition (60 economies, 10-12.5%) that resolved July 24 remains in force; USMCA-qualifying goods stay exempt from Section 301.

label: Global Policy Uncertainty / Recession Risk
value: SEPT 2: Global Bond Yield Rout Hits Multi-Decade Highs (US, Japan, Germany, UK) as Mideast Strikes Reignite and ADP Shows Hiring Slowdown
source: Federal Reserve / ADP / ISM / China NBS / Census Bureau / U. Michigan; July 17 – September 2, 2026
delta: AUG 31-SEPT 2 ARC: Renewed US-Iran strikes and tanker attacks near the Strait of Hormuz reignited the oil/inflation channel, driving a synchronized global government bond selloff to multi-decade highs even as ADP flagged a sharp US private-hiring slowdown — a stagflation-adjacent combination that raises, rather than lowers, near-term recession risk.
deltaNote: SEPT 2 RECESSION RISK SNAPSHOT: The dominant new risk channel is a globally synchronized bond yield rout — US 10Y at 4.814% (highest since Nov 2023), Japan's 10Y above 3% for the first time since 1996, Germany's Bund at 3.375% (highest since 2011), and UK gilts at 5.25% (highest since 2008) — driven by renewed Strait of Hormuz strikes (oil tankers hit Aug 31-Sept 1, Brent to $94.65) reigniting inflation fears just as ADP showed private payrolls slowing to 38,000 in August (from 46,000) and the ISM Manufacturing PMI cooled to 54.6%. Tightening financial conditions (higher yields) combined with softening labor and manufacturing data is the classic pre-recession mix analysts flag as most concerning. Also in play: an active US-Canada trade war (Canada's retaliatory tariffs effective Sept 8), a deepening China slowdown, and elevated equity valuations that shrugged off the yield spike Sept 2. Next catalysts: BLS August jobs report (Friday Sept 4) and the September 16-17 FOMC meeting.

label: BOJ Policy Rate
source: Bank of Japan, June 16 2026 (25bp hike — highest since 1995)
deltaNote: June 16: BOJ hiked 25bp to 1.00%, the highest level since 1995, in a 7-1 vote (Asada dissenting) — citing Iran-war energy-cost pass-through risk. The hike landed the same day Warsh's first FOMC opened, raising August-2024-style carry-unwind concerns; the immediate market reaction was orderly (Nikkei +0.46%), but the yen still fell to a fresh 40-year low past 162/USD by June 30 despite the hike and an estimated $72.5bn in prior FX intervention.
